title: Investigating Role of Electron Correlation Effects via Triple Excitations for Precise Evaluation of Energies and Hyperfine Structure Constants in $^{23}$Na
abstract: Accurate determination of hyperfine structure constants in atomic systems provides important insight into the interplay of electron correlation and relativistic effects in the nuclear region. Although sodium (Na) is a relatively light atom, previous all-order relativistic many-body calculations of the magnetic dipole hyperfine constants for the low-lying states of $^{23}$Na show noticeable discrepancies with experiment. To address this, we calculate the ionization potentials and hyperfine structure constants of $^{23}$Na using relativistic coupled-cluster theory with explicit inclusion of triple excitations. We further incorporate corrections from the Breit interaction, quantum electrodynamics, and the Bohr-Weisskopf (BW) effect. Results from lower-order methods are also presented to assess the importance of different physical contributions across states. Our calculations demonstrate that contributions from the lower-order relativistic and BW effects play almost similar roles with the electron correlation effects, including triple excitations, and are essential for reconciling theoretical predictions with experimental observations. This study can also serve as a useful guide for understanding the role of triples in heavier alkali systems.
summary: This paper performs high-precision theoretical calculations on the hyperfine structure constants of sodium using advanced relativistic coupled-cluster methods. By systematically including triple excitations and various QED/relativistic corrections, the authors demonstrate that these higher-order terms are crucial for matching theory to experimental measurements. The study provides a detailed roadmap for calculating atomic properties in light alkali metals.
main_problem: The study aims to accurately determine hyperfine structure constants (HFS) and ionization potentials for the sodium atom by systematically investigating the role of electron correlation effects, particularly those arising from triple excitations.
main_result: Including contributions from triple excitations, along with Breit, QED, and Bohr-Weisskopf corrections, is essential for reconciling theoretical predictions of HFS constants with precise experimental measurements in $^{23}	ext{Na}$.
method: The authors employ relativistic coupled-cluster theory (RCCSDT) alongside various lower-order many-body perturbation theories (RMBPT) to treat electron correlation effects.
model_or_system: The system is the sodium atom ($^{23}	ext{Na}$), treated using a Dirac-Coulomb Hamiltonian. The calculations involve incorporating relativistic corrections like the Breit interaction and QED effects into the many-body framework.
key_observables: Hyperfine structure constants (magnetic dipole $A_{	ext{hf}}$ and electric quadrupole $B_{	ext{hf}}$) and Ionization Potentials (IPs).
important_parameters: The relative magnitude of correlation effects versus relativistic/higher-order terms; the importance of triple excitations.
main_assumptions: The calculations rely on approximations inherent to many-body theory, such as truncating the excitation series (e.g., $	ext{RCCSDT}$), though they systematically compare these limits.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the systematic inclusion of different physical processes (correlation effects) in S and P states compared to D states, showing how corrections contribute significantly to $A_{	ext{hf}}$ constants.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by establishing the theoretical framework using relativistic coupled-cluster theory. It then systematically compares results obtained from various levels of approximation ($	ext{DHF} ightarrow 	ext{RMBPT}(2) ightarrow \dots ightarrow 	ext{RCCSDT}$) while incorporating multiple high-precision corrections (Breit, QED, BW).
why_interesting: This work exemplifies state-of-the-art theoretical atomic structure calculations, providing crucial benchmarks for understanding how electron correlation and relativistic effects manifest in measurable quantities like HFS constants.
